title: Redwood technical deep dive - dedicated vs hosted (runtime, KV cache, batching)
summary: Redwood AE+SE ran a deep technical session with AtlasData to compare dedicated vs hosted modes. Discussion covered runtime optimizations (kernel selection, attention cache), KV prefix caching, workload-aware batching, quantization tradeoffs, and VPC/on-prem constraints. AtlasData cares about predictable throughput for real-time scoring, tenant isolation concerns, SOC2/KMS, and benchmarking steps. Actionable next steps: run a 2-week dedicated benchmark, share security pack, and proposal for dedicated capacity sizing.
next_steps: Redwood to share dedicated vs hosted benchmark spreadsheet and test harness link
AtlasData to provide 2 representative workloads and sample prompts for KV-cache profiling
Schedule pilot kickoff w/ infra and security (proposed week of 2026-04-06)
Redwood to send security and SOC2 docs and KMS integration notes
transcript:
[00:00] Alex (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. We got Alex and Samir from Redwood, thanks for coordinating AtlasData. Quick agenda: runtime performance, KV cache behavior, batching and quantization, then VPC/on-prem and isolation concerns.
[00:18] Jordan (AtlasData - Head of ML): Yep, thanks. We want to understand tradeoffs: our main requirement is sub-120ms p50 for single-turn scoring at 512 tokens and steady throughput of ~300 qps per tenant. We have multi-tenant loads, worried about noisy neighbor.
[00:34] Samir (Redwood SE): Great, that gives a target. Quick callout: p50 vs p95 matters for tail. In hosted we do cross-tenant multiplexing and dynamic routing, in Dedicated you get reserved GPU pools with isolation and deterministic throughput.
[00:52] Ravi (Infra): When you say "reserved", what does that mean for noisy neighbors? We don't want another tenant bursting to push our latency up.
[01:05] Samir: Dedicated = you own a pool, noisy neighbor is effectively within your org only. If you have multiple teams inside AtlasData we can still do per-route isolation and RBAC. In hosted, we cap tokens and use QoS; we also have automatic fallback to cheaper model shards if contention happens but that can change quality.
[01:28] Marta (Security): Also needs to be clear about audit logs and KMS. We have to show key separation for encryption in transit and at rest.
[01:36] Alex: We will send the security pack. We support customer-managed KMS and HSM for Private/Dedicated; hosted uses Redwood-managed keys by default but customer KMS is available for enterprise accounts.
[01:52] Ethan (Eng Lead): Can we talk about KV cache? We have long context prompts, and cold-starts are killing our latency. Is KV cache per-request, per-tenant, or global?
[02:05] Samir: Good question. The KV cache is per-runtime instance and keyed by model+input-prefix; we do prefix caching where frequent prefixes are sticky in memory. On Dedicated you can choose longer cache retention and pinning; hosted uses eviction policies tuned for multi-tenant fairness. Note: sometimes transcription says "KV cash" in old notes, I've seen that.
[02:24] Jordan: So if we have repeated prompt templates across tenants, hosted might evict ours under load?
[02:31] Samir: Correct, in hosted the cache is workload-aware but not tenant-reserved. For strict cache guarantees you want Dedicated or Private.
[02:40] [00:02:40] Alex: Let's dig into batching. We do continuous batching in the runtime — dynamic batching that tries to combine similar sequence lengths and keep latency SLOs.
[02:55] Samir: The key knobs: max batch size, batch wait (ms), per-model quantization profile. For low-latency scoring, you often reduce batch wait and decrease max batch size which increases GPU inefficiency but lowers tail latency. For throughput-oriented workloads, increase batch wait to improve GPU utilization.
[03:17] Ravi: Any rules of thumb numbers?
[03:20] Samir: For a 300 qps steady workload at 512 tokens, on A100-like hardware (single model) we'd recommend initial batch size 16-32 and batch wait 5-10ms; Dedicated lets you tune aggressively because you won't be impacted by cross-tenant mixing. Hosted uses more conservative defaults to avoid one tenant monopolizing.
[03:39] Nina (Data Scientist): How does quantization affect quality for our LLM-2 style models? We use a finetuned open model.
[03:47] Samir: We support int8 and experimental 4-bit profiles. Quantization reduces memory and increases throughput but may introduce output drift. We run accuracy regressions using your eval sets; often int8 is safe for many tasks, 4-bit requires careful validation. We'll surface per-model regressed metrics.
[04:05] Jordan: Are those quantized kernels run differently between hosted and dedicated?
[04:09] Samir: Kernels are the same, but Dedicated can pin specific kernel variants and compiler flags per pool which can extract extra p50 improvements. Hosted chooses kernels per-request for safety and compatibility.
[04:24] [00:04:24] Alex: On noisy neighbor and isolation, Dedicated gives predictable throughput SLAs. We offer throughput guarantees as part of Reserved Capacity contracts — e.g., X tokens/sec at Y latency targets; if we violate, SLA credits apply. Hosted doesn't offer the same hard guarantees.
[04:44] Ethan: How do you measure those guarantees? Do you provide a test harness?
[04:48] Lee (SRE): Yes, we have a benchmark harness (link: https://redwood.ai/benchmarks/dedicated-vs-hosted) and a replay tool you can run against both hosted and Dedicated endpoints. We'll share the script. It simulates realistic concurrency and variable seq lengths and captures p50/p95/p99 and GPU utilization.
[05:05] Jordan: Nice. For our compliance people, we'd like the replay artifacts to be reproducible and run inside our VPC where possible.
[05:12] Lee: For Private deployments we can run the harness inside your VPC or on-prem; for Dedicated we can provide a private network peering so you can run the replay from your infra while hitting Dedicated endpoints. Hosted can only be tested from our public endpoints or peered networks with secure tunnels.
[05:28] Marta: SOC2 and audit logs — will the log retention change between hosted and dedicated?
[05:33] Alex: Hosted has default retention windows; Dedicated/Private can increase retention and provide raw audit logs. We can also route logs to your SIEM via secure forwarding.
[05:43] [00:05:43] Samir: Back to runtime internals: cache invalidation and KV eviction policies. We expose metrics: cache_hit_ratio, cache_evictions, avg_kv_latency. On Dedicated you can tune cache size and pin frequently used keys. On hosted we tune automatically to balance fairness. We also show per-route cache metrics in the console.
[06:05] Ravi: If I pin keys, is that memory isolated per-tenant?
[06:09] Samir: On Dedicated yes; on hosted pinning is soft and subject to global pressure. Pinning in Dedicated ensures those prefixes stay resident, which helps cold-start and reduces tail.
[06:18] Nina: Are your caches sharded across GPUs or per-process? How does it behave with multi-GPU model parallelism?
[06:25] Samir: Good question. KV storage lives in local runtime memory per model shard; with multi-GPU we coordinate via a distributed KV layer that maintains coherence. There are extra round trips for cross-shard fetches; Dedicated setups with model sharding on a single host reduce that overhead.
[06:41] Jordan: That sounds like a big reason we'd go Dedicated if we want multi-GPU sharded models.
[06:46] Samir: Exactly. For heavy multi-GPU, Dedicated or Private gives you more control over placement and pinned caches.
[06:52] [00:06:52] Alex: Let's talk about rollback and model variants. If a hosted endpoint degrades, we may fallback to smaller variants. In Dedicated you can configure canaries and A/B rollouts with automatic fallback to a specific pinned variant.
[07:08] Ethan: For our use cases we can't have fallbacks change semantics unexpectedly; how would we test rollouts?
[07:14] Jess (Product): We recommend canary traffic percentages and then validate via automated evals tied to your golden prompts. We can integrate evals into the rollout pipeline and block rollouts if quality drops beyond thresholds.
[07:28] Jordan: What about cost considerations? You mentioned Dedicated is more expensive but predictable. Any numbers?
[07:36] Alex: Roughly, Dedicated has a fixed monthly commit for reserved GPUs plus usage for extra burst; hosted is purely usage-based. For large steady workloads Dedicated typically reduces per-token cost by 20-40% depending on utilization. We'll share a sizing/cost spreadsheet.
[07:52] [00:07:52] Samir: Another nuance: batching dynamics in Dedicated let you push batch sizes higher which increases throughput but may slightly raise p95. You can do hybrid: Reserved pool with a small hosted overflow for spiky traffic.
[08:05] Ravi: Hybrid sounds interesting. How is overflow handled network-wise?
[08:09] Lee: Overflow routing is policy-based. Requests are routed to Dedicated first, if capacity constraints hit a threshold we route to hosted-compatible variants or scale up Dedicated if autoscaling configured. Policies are per-route.
[08:23] Marta: For legal/procurement, what's the procurement path for Dedicated? Do you require long-term contract?
[08:29] Alex: We offer monthly and annual reserved options. Annual gives better pricing and capacity reservations. Procurement steps are standard: NDA, SOW, SOC2 documentation. We can start with a timeboxed pilot before signing long-term.
[08:43] [00:08:43] Jordan: Can you walk us through a specific benchmark scenario? Something that mirrors our 300 qps at ~512 tokens.
[08:49] Samir: Sure. We'll spin a Dedicated pool with 4x A100 equivalents, pin the model, enable int8 quantization profile if your eval tolerates it, set batch_size target 32, batch_wait 8ms, and run the replay at increasing concurrency until latency SLOs break. We capture per-tenant throughput and GPU utilization.
[09:11] Nina: For our finetuned model, how much does int8 typically change accuracy? We've seen small drops in F1 for some classification tasks.
[09:19] Samir: It depends. For generation heavy tasks we see low drift for int8, but for nuanced classification you should run the eval harness. We'll instrument rouge/bleu/F1 diffs for your golden set. If int8 fails, try mixed precision or per-layer quantization.
[09:34] [00:09:34] Ethan: What's the timeline to run a pilot and get data back?
[09:38] Alex: Once we have prompts, we can provision a Dedicated test pool in ~3-5 business days, run a 2-week benchmark, and deliver a report. For Private/on-prem add provisioning time.
[09:51] Jordan: Provision time good. For VPC peering and network egress we need to verify data residency.
[09:56] Lee: We support VPC peering and private link; egress billing and routing policies can be configured. We'll include network diagrams in the security pack.
[10:07] Marta: Do you provide SOC2 scope details for Dedicated vs Hosted? Some customers require dedicated infra in-scope of their audits.
[10:14] Alex: We'll include the SOC2 report and scoping notes. Dedicated/Private gives you more control for audit evidence; hosted has standard SOC2 controls but less direct artifact access.
[10:26] [00:10:26] Samir: Performance tuning tips: 1) warm your KV cache with a small warmup workload, 2) use shorter tokens or chunking for scoring tasks to reduce end-to-end token counts, 3) tune batch wait and batch size per workload, 4) prefer Dedicated for sharded multi-GPU to reduce cross-shard KV fetches.
[10:47] Jordan: Warmups — do you recommend a constant keep-alive traffic to keep model memory primed?
[10:53] Samir: A small periodic warmup is helpful; we also support cold start warmup flows where the runtime preloads KV entries for pinned prompts. In Dedicated you can increase memory retention windows.
[11:04] Nina: Any caveats for function calling and streaming in Dedicated?
[11:09] Samir: Streaming is supported both places. For function/tool calls that trigger external I/O, network time dominates. For streaming low-latency use cases Dedicated reduces server-side p50 but external dependencies still matter.
[11:22] [00:11:22] Ethan: We have a question about per-tenant throttles. Can we set per-route quotas to prevent internal teams from hogging Dedicated resources?
[11:29] Jess: Yes, policy controls allow per-route quotas, rate limits, and priorities. You can also attach billing tags for internal chargeback.
[11:37] Jordan: How granular are observability metrics? We need token-level billing and per-route latency breakdowns.
[11:42] Lee: Console exposes token-level cost, per-model latency histograms, per-route traces and KV metrics. For Dedicated we can increase retention and provide raw telemetry exports to your S3 or SIEM.
[11:58] [00:11:58] Marta: A quick security edge case: if we use customer-managed KMS, how is key access managed for Redwood operators?
[12:05] Alex: With customer-managed KMS we never hold plaintext keys. Access is via envelope encryption; Redwood operators don't get key material. For Private/on-prem keys stay in your HSM. We'll include diagrams and IAM roles in the pack.
[12:20] Jordan: Back to benchmarks: can we run the replay in our VPC against a Dedicated pool?
[12:24] Lee: Yes, with peering/private link we support that. We'll provide the replay container.
[12:30] [00:12:30] Ravi: Any caveat about model updates? If we pin a model and you push a new version, how is rollout managed?
[12:36] Samir: Rollouts are explicit. We only auto-update if you opt in. You can pin versions per-route; we also support canary traffic and automatic rollback based on eval metrics.
[12:48] Jordan: Great. One more: what's the expected variance in p95 when moving from hosted to Dedicated?
[12:55] Samir: Typical p95 reduction is 15-40% depending on workload characteristics and contention. Dedicated removes cross-tenant headroom variability and lets you tune batching and cache pinning which tightens tails. We'll show concrete numbers in the benchmark report.
[13:11] [00:13:11] Alex: Ok let's run through a proposed pilot plan: 1) AtlasData shares two representative workloads and golden prompts, 2) Redwood provisions a Dedicated test pool, 3) run 2-week benchmark (replay + evals), 4) produce report with cost/latency/quality and recommended config.
[13:28] Jordan: Sounds good. Any blockers on our side?
[13:31] Marta: Need security docs and SOW for legal.
[13:34] Alex: We'll email the security pack and SOW template.
[13:38] Nina: When we run evals, what's the format for outputs? JSON lines?
[13:42] Samir: We accept JSONL with fields for prompt, expected, and metrics; we'll share the schema.
[13:49] Ethan: If we find quantization causes quality regressions can we fall back to mixed precision quickly?
[13:54] Samir: Yes, you can switch quant profiles per-route and roll back.
[13:58] [00:13:58] Lee: Small infra note: if you want model pinned to a single host we can provision that for Dedicated but it affects redundancy; we recommend cross-host replication with sticky caches for high availability.
[14:13] Jordan: For HA, if a host dies, how quick is failover and cache warmup impact?
[14:18] Samir: Failover is automated; however cold cache rebuild will increase p95 temporarily. For critical workloads we recommend active-active across zones with cache warming policies.
[14:33] Marta: Legal will ask about egress logs and data deletion.
[14:36] Alex: We'll include data retention, deletion API, and egress policy details in the pack.
[14:43] [00:14:43] Jess: Quick recap of config knobs we discussed: batch_size, batch_wait_ms, cache_size/pinning, quant_profile, routing policy, per-route quotas, canary percentages.
[14:58] Jordan: Can you share example config for our 300 qps use-case?
[15:02] Samir: We'll attach a template: start with batch_size 32, batch_wait 8ms, pin top 50 prefixes, int8 trial, and a replay script.
[15:12] Nina: Anything else about on-prem? We have a locked-down environment; can you support air-gapped installs?
[15:18] Alex: Yes, Private/on-prem supports air-gapped installs; it requires extra lead time and a different licensing model. We'll include that path in the SOW.
[15:27] [00:15:27] Ethan: Do you have references or customers who've run similar pilots?
[15:30] Alex: We can share anonymized win stories and contact refs under NDA.
[15:36] Jordan: Ok, let's call out explicit next steps and owners.
[15:40] Alex: Sure. We'll put them in the follow-up email.
[15:44] [00:15:44] -- brief pause while notes captured --
[16:00] Jordan: Quick follow-up: for throughput guarantees, if you provide X tokens/sec SLA and you miss, what's the typical SLA credit?
[16:08] Alex: Credits are contract-specific; typical formula is prorated monthly service fee based on time under the SLA. We'll include standard SLA terms in the SOW.
[16:20] Ravi: One technical nit: you mentioned distributed KV coherence for sharded models — do you use RDMA or gRPC for cross-shard fetches?
[16:28] Samir: We use a mix: within-host we use shared memory/RDMA-like channels; cross-host we use low-latency RPCs with protobufs. Those calls add overhead; minimizing cross-shard fetches is why single-host sharded placement is beneficial in Dedicated.
[16:47] Nina: Do you support sparse attention kernels or flash attention variants?
[16:52] Samir: We support multiple attention kernels and select based on model arch and seq length. For long-context workloads flash attention often helps; we'll recommend kernel profiles in the benchmark.
[17:04] [00:17:04] Jordan: Any final questions from AtlasData?
[17:07] Ethan: Just one — can we get per-tenant isolation guarantees documented for Dedicated?
[17:12] Alex: Yes, we'll include isolation docs showing memory and kernel pinning, RBAC, and per-route quotas.
[17:19] Jordan: Perfect. Thanks everyone.
[17:22] Alex: Thanks all. We'll send the security pack, benchmark harness, and a proposed pilot timeline.
[17:28] -- call ends --
